English: The heroes entered the city and swiftly went to their homes, the kings of the earth engaged in their respective duties. The houses of the city officials and the charioteers were also approached by them. The sons of Pāṇḍu, having been honored by the citizens, went to the abode prepared by Purochana. Purochana provided them with food, drink, auspicious beds, and main seats. There, they were greatly honored, covered with fine garments, and worshipped by the city dwellers. After ten nights had passed, Purochana then announced the house named Hivākhya. There, the tiger-like men, adorned with various garments, were engaged in conversation, as per Purochana's words, like the Guhyakas. Considering the essence of the matter, Yudhishthira spoke to Bhīma, saying, "Desiring the fragrant food mixed with ghee, This has indeed been prepared for the fire, O scorcher of enemies, brought forth for the household duties." The materials like munja grass and others, were all smeared with ghee.

English: 536 Jatugṛhadāhapavaṁ By the good deeds of the righteous, O king, I am consumed by the sin of desire for destruction. Then, having seen that great wise moon, I was addressed by him in the past regarding the calamity. We, having been enlightened by him, are wise and have entered the house of the wise, supported by the teachers and the good deeds of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Bhīma said: If this house is indeed meant for burning, let us go there where we have previously resided. Yudhishṭhira said: Here, it is pleasing to you to say that it should not be rejected. Like the loss, we are searching for the desired path, surely. If our enemy, the one who is the architect of our destruction, finds it, he will quickly become fierce and burn us. This one does not fear the outcry of the wicked, nor does he fear the wrath of the architect of our destruction. Thus, indeed, the foolish Suyodhana remains steadfast in his opinion. Even if Bhīṣma, our grandfather, is among those who are burned, who will provoke him, or who will anger him? Thus, indeed, the Kauravas may become angry.

English: Jatugṛhadāhapavaṁ Concealed, Vidura spoke: "You are the best among the Pāṇḍavas. What shall I do for you with confidence?" In the dark of the Krishna Paksha, the fire will consume your house. The Pāṇḍavas, who are like men, should be burned along with their mother. Thus, I have heard from Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Moreover, Vidura spoke: "You are indeed a Pāṇḍava, as you have been told this for the sake of trust." Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, with steadfastness, said to him: "I recognize you, dear friend of Vidura." It is always pleasing and dear, and there is no need for the poet's knowledge. As we are, so are you; we are in your protection. This is my opinion: I shall take refuge in you, as directed by the orders of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. That sinful Kaurava and his allies constantly trouble us. May you deliver us from this fire, for indeed, Duryodhana is desirous of our destruction.

English: This prosperous armory belongs to that wicked one. In the pit, this great deed has been done without any remedy. This indeed is certainly what he desires. Long ago, Vidura knew this and informed us. This calamity has come upon us, which you have seen before. You should release us from the fear of Purōchana. Thus he promised, and the miner, having dug, made a great noise. In the middle of the wheel, the face is not very large, and the door is unknown, equal to the earth, O Bhārata. Out of fear of Purōchana, he covered his face. There he always resides at the house door. There, all the armed ones lived, O King, during the night. By day, they roamed in the forest, the sons of Pāṇḍu. Trustworthy yet untrustworthy, they deceive Purōchana. Dissatisfied, the king, like one who is very unhappy. The townspeople did not understand him. Elsewhere, Vidura's mother came from the best of miners.

English: The sage spoke. Seeing them, the wise Sumanasa became angry. Purocana, having perceived them as trustworthy, became joyful. Then, when Purocana was pleased, Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, Bhīma, and Arjuna spoke. This wicked Purocana knows us well. I think this cruel soul is deceived in his escape. After lighting the armory and burning Purocana, the six brothers did not remain unscathed. Then, by the order of Dāna, Kuntī prepared a feast for the Brahmins. Many women came there. After enjoying as they pleased, having released and drunk, O Bhārata, they granted permission to Madhavī as if she were a household. The five sons of the Nishāda, however, were invited to that feast. The hungry one, urged by time, came with her sons. Having drunk wine, intoxicated, with her sons, she was bewildered. And the king, in that very place, was not aware. The king, devoid of knowledge, slept like a dead man. Then, in the night, when the wind blew, the people slept. The house of Jatu was set ablaze.

English: The wise one lies where Purochana is. Then a great sound of valor arose from the assembly, and the people became aware of it. The people said: By the wickedness of Duryodhana, with a mind devoid of wisdom, the house was constructed and set ablaze for the destruction of the self. Alas, how lamentable is the wisdom of Dhṛtarāṣṭra! He who burned the pure Pandavas in their home. By fate, now the sinful one is caught, this extremely foolish one, who did not burn the noble men who were trustworthy. Veraṁpāyana said: Thus, the people of Vārāṇasī lamented, surrounding the house, they stood all night. The Pandavas, along with their mother, were also very distressed, and they went out through the hole that was made. Due to the disturbance of sleep and the fear of the Pandavas, they could not go out suddenly with their mother, O scorcher of enemies. But Bhīma, the king, with the speed of Bhīma, went to call his brothers and his mother. Having lifted his mother, the valiant one went.

English: The Nishādī saw the burned one, the five sons of Anāga. With a shovel, he searched the hole, covered with dust, marked by a man. Then the citizens of Dhṛtarāṣṭra sent forth, along with the Pāṇḍavas, the burned minister Purochana. Hearing this, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the king, was greatly distressed by the destruction of the Pāṇḍu sons. Today, my brother, the king, who is very rare, is dead among those heroes who were burned, along with the mother. Let the men go quickly to the city of Vāraṇavat, and honor those heroes and Kuntī's son. Let them also make the auspicious and great wells, and let them also honor the friends of those who died there. Thus, I can do whatever is beneficial, let everything be done for the Pāṇḍavas and Kuntī. Thus, Uttava, surrounded by relatives, made arrangements for the Pāṇḍu sons, the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra and Ambikā. All the Kauravas were very much overcome with grief. Vidura, though less, also felt great sorrow. The Pāṇḍavas, having exited the city of Vāraṇavat, swiftly took refuge in the southern direction.

English: Thus, having approached the trees, the mighty one went. The Pandavas were born from the earth. Again, he was far away, hidden on the path due to the fear of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. With great difficulty, he carried his one delicate and glorious mother there, amidst obstacles. You will come to a forest area with little roots, fruits, and water, where a fierce bird-like beast roams in the evening, O Bharata. The dreadful twilight became fierce with the cries of beasts and birds; the directions were dark and the wind was close. They were tormented by fatigue and thirst, unable to move due to sleep. Then Bhīma entered the terrible forest, a vast wilderness, approaching a large banyan tree with ample shade, beautiful to behold. There, having placed them down, the best of the Bharatas spoke: "I am going to hunt; rest here, my lord." These creatures cry sweetly, the waterfowl with matted feathers; indeed, this is a great truth. Having received permission, he went, as his elder brother Bharata said, to where the waterfowl cry.

English: 546 Jatugṛhadāhapavaṁ He, having drunk water there, O best of the Bharatas, then took water with his upper garment, O king. 013 Having come quickly from the cow's measure, he saw his mother, who was asleep, on the ground. 014 The grief-stricken Bhīma lamented. 014 In the past, those who were in the city of Vārāṇasī did not awaken from their sleep; today they are asleep on the ground. 015 The sister of Vasudeva, the destroyer of enemies, Kuntī, adorned with all auspicious marks. 016 The beautiful and valorous Bhīma, the great-souled Pāṇḍava, always lay in the palace, shining like a lotus. 017 The very delicate and thin one, suitable for a great bed, lay on the earth, not suitable for such a bed. 018 The earth, exhausted, gave birth to these sons of Indra and Vāyu; this earth, indeed, is weeping, as it is not suitable. 019 What could be more painful for me to see than this? I, who today am RATA GAIAM on the ground. 020 In the three worlds, a king who is worthy of the knowledge of heat. This earth, indeed, is weeping; how could it be like a common man? 021 This one, dark like a blue cloud, unmatched among men on earth, is weeping; how could it be more painful than a common man? 022

English: The gods, like the Ashvins, are endowed with beauty; they are like the earth, lying in slumber. Those who are not known are difficult to recognize, like the Kurus; one lives happily in the village like a solitary FA. One tree in the village bears fruits; it becomes a sanctuary for the known, like Agta. Many brave ones, known for their adherence to dharma, live happily in the world and are free from ailments. The strong, prosperous, and friendly ones live by relying on each other, like the denizens of the forest. We, however, have been exiled by Dhṛtarāṣṭra and his wicked son; we are not burned by his rule. Therefore, we are freed from the burning tree; what path shall we take to attain the highest bliss? Not far from the city, I see a forest; one must remain awake while the other sleeps. While I am observing, the wise one, having conquered the mind, is indeed Bhīma, who woke up then.

English: Having killed these men, bring them to my presence. There is fear for you from the great lords of our domain. Having prepared the flesh of these men as desired, I will eat it along with grass, as per my words. Understanding the words of her brother, the Rakṣasī hurriedly went to the place where the sons of Pāṇḍu, the best of the Bharatas, were. There, having arrived, she saw the Pāṇḍavas with Pṛthā, Bhīma, who was awake and unconquered. She saw Bhīma, like a mountain, and desired him in the form of a beautiful woman. This dark-skinned one, with great arms, with a lion-like body and great radiance, will be mine. I will never heed my brother's cruel words, for he is not as strong as my brother's companion. For a moment, satisfaction and the ability to kill will arise. Having killed him, I will rejoice for eternal years. She, taking the form of a beautiful woman, approached the great-armed Bhīma slowly. As if entwined with a creeper, adorned with divine ornaments, she spoke this smiling sentence to Bhīma.

English: Where have you come from, O best of men? Who are you? These men here are in the form of gods. What is this great dark maiden, O sinless one? She shines like this forest, having reached her own home. This dense forest, served by demons, is not known to anyone. Here lives a sinful demon named Hidiṃba. I have been sent here by my brother, with the wicked intention of the demon, to devour your flesh like that of immortals. I do not wish for any other husband, O divine one, I speak the truth. Knowing this, act accordingly with me, O one whose mind is disturbed by desire, serve me. I am afraid of you, O great-armed one, from the demon and the man. O son, be my protector in this perilous situation. I wander in the sky, as I desire, and attain unmatched joy there with you. Bhīma said: Who would abandon his mother, elder brother, and younger brothers, when born in a demon? Who indeed, when asleep, would eat the food of demons, like a man who is blind to his mother? The killing of Hidiṃba.

English: Hidiṃba said: "Frightened, this is what Bhīma said." "This wicked soul is attacking; I will act as a brother to you, so do as I say." "I am desirous and accompanied by a host of demons; I will take you to my abode, leaving no one behind." "Awaken those who are asleep, O scorcher of foes; I will go with you all, taking you without leaving anyone behind." Bhīma said: "Do not fear, O one with broad hips; no one can stand against me. I will kill this one, O fair one." "This cowardly demon is not a match for me in battle." "Behold my arms, well-formed like an elephant's trunk; my thighs are like iron clubs, and my chest is well-built." "You will see my prowess like that of Indra; do not underestimate me, thinking I am merely a human." Hidiṃba said: "I do not belittle you, O man-lion; I see you as a demon among men." "Verily, I am a demon who has come to kill Hidiṃba."

English: Thus, while Bhīma was speaking, the man-eater Hal heard his words. Observing the human form of Hidiṃba, adorned with a garland and having a face like a full moon, with beautiful eyebrows, gentle nails, and dressed in fine garments, he became angry at the beautiful human form she was bearing. The demon, Hidiṃba, who was strong, spoke to her, "Who is this fool who obstructs my desire?" "Do you not fear Hidiṃba, who is enraged and has been deceived by my anger? I will destroy you, who are a source of trouble for me, and all the powerful demons before me." Thus, Hidiṃba, with fierce eyes, prepared to attack him, baring his teeth. Seeing him rushing forward, Bhīma, the mighty one, prepared to strike, saying, "Stand firm, stand firm!"

English: The elephant's foot crushes the strong. Today, the flesh will be devoured by the vultures and the dogs. Let them rejoice on the ground, having been slain by me in battle. Today, I will clear this thorny forest in an instant. It is always polluted by you who devour men. Today, my sister, you will see me, having been captured by me, like a great serpent. Unhindered by you, having been slain by me, the men who wander in the forest will roam this forest. Hidimba said: What is the use of your boasting, O man, with your empty words? Do not delay in doing this deed. You think of yourself as strong, but I will know your true strength when we meet. I will not let these men sleep as they wish. I will kill you, O foolish one, who speaks unkindly. Having drunk from your sweet limbs, I will then kill this one who acts unfavorably. Vērāmpāyana said: Having spoken thus, the strong man seized the arms of the man.

English: The astonished men, like tigers among men, were with Pṛthā. Then Kuntī, seeing them, astonished by their beauty, spoke this sweet word gently to them. "Who are you, O beautiful one, in the guise of a celestial? By what means, O well-formed one, have you come here?" "If you are a deity of the forest or a celestial, tell me the whole truth, why do you stand here?" Hidimba spoke: "This great forest, resembling a blue cloud, is the abode of the demon, and it belongs to me, Hidimba." "Know me, O beautiful one, as the sister of the lord of demons; I have been sent here by my brother, who wishes to kill you and your son." "Having heard his cruel words, I came here; I did not see your son, who is of great splendor." "Then, while wandering in the presence of all beings, I was compelled by your son, who is under the influence of Manmatha." "Then, surrounded by me, your son, the mighty one, was trying to take me, but I could not." "Knowing me to be long-lived, that man came himself to kill all your kin."

English: Hidimbavadha's glory He, with my beloved and your wise son, was forcefully defeated by the great-souled one. With great speed, he and the elephant-like ones were pulling each other in battle, like man-eating demons. Vyāsa spoke: Upon hearing her words, Yudhishthira arose, along with Arjuna, Nakula, and the mighty Sahadeva. They saw each other, engaged in battle, like lions in a fierce fight. While pulling each other, they created a cloud of dust, like a fire surrounded by smoke. Just as the earth is enveloped by the earth-holder, may it shine like the sun covered by mist. Seeing Bhīma, the man-eater spoke this, laughing: "Bhīma, O mighty one, we do not know you. We are all asleep, like those in the form of Bhīma." "I am here to assist; I will fight the demon. Nakula and Sahadeva will protect our mother." Bhīma spoke.

English: Be indifferent and observe; do not act, for you are confused. If you are reborn, it will be due to my influence. Arjuna said: What is the use of Bhīma living long with the sinful demon? It is not possible to stay here for long. In the past, the east was adorned, and the evening was approaching. The powerful demons are indeed present. Hasten, Bhīma; do not play; kill the demon Vibhīṣaṇa. In the past, he created an illusion with his arms. Vērāmpāyana said: Thus addressed by Arjuna, Bhīma, the son of Bhīma, lifted the body of the demon and threw it into the hermitage with great strength. Bhīma said: You are indeed a fool; you are strong in vain, old in vain, and your thoughts are in vain. You do not deserve to die in vain; you will not be in vain today. Arjuna said: Or do you think that you will bear this burden of the demon in battle? I will assist you; let him be killed quickly. Or I myself will kill him, O Vṛkodara. Having done so, I am indeed exhausted; let us rest for a while.

English: 562 Bakavadhapava Even with a boon, you too, O swift one, At that time, she who speaks thus indeed rejects the action. 008 Whether you consider me foolish or as a devotee following you, O great one, unite me with your son. 009 Taking him, I shall go to the divine form as I wish, I shall return again; grant me confidence. 010 I indeed meditate with my mind; I shall always protect you. I shall save the bulls in distress. 011 I shall carry you on my back swiftly, desiring speed. You all do me a favor; let Bhīma serve me. 012 In times of danger, he who holds onto righteousness is the best knower of dharma. Indeed, calamity is said to be the distress of the righteous. 013 He who protects life in virtue is said to be virtuous; By whomsoever dharma is practiced, in him, there is no sin. 014 Yudhiṣṭhira said: Thus, as it is, you should stay here, O Hidimba; You should remain here as I have said, O sweet one. 015 O auspicious one, having done the auspicious act, You should worship Bhīma, before the journey begins. 016

English: As you wish, O mind-speeding one, Bhīma will always be brought to you at night. Thus, knowing this, the demoness Hidiṃbā then approached Bhīma. In beautiful abodes of the gods, in delightful places filled with deer and birds, Adorned with the finest form and decorations, she sweetly conversed with the Pāṇḍava. Similarly, in forest fortresses, in flowering groves, In beautiful lakes adorned with lotuses, In river islands and sandy shores, In sacred waters of the forest and in mountain rivers, In the regions of Sagara, in places filled with jewels and gold, In beautiful towns and great sal forests, In sacred divine forests and in the pure banks of rivers, In the abodes of the Guhyakas and in the hermitages, Holding a supreme form, she delighted the Pāṇḍava. Thus, delighting Bhīma, she moved here and there, O mind-speeding one.

English: He recognized the powerful son of the demon, Bhīma. With the deformed eyes, the great demon, Rāṅukaṇa, and Vibhīṣaṇa. The mighty archer, the great hero, the one of great strength, the one with great arms, the one of great speed, the one of great body, the one of great illusion. The inhuman, human-like, Bhīma-like, and very strong. He who overcomes the demons is a human. Even a child, upon reaching youth, among humans, O lord of the world. In all forms, he is the greatest hero, he became prominent. Indeed, the demons in the womb receive and give birth. Those who take on forms of desire also become many-shaped. Bowing down, he grasped the feet of his father. And of his mother, the supreme archer, he also named him Chakratu. He spoke to his mother, "It is Ghaṭa-bhāsa." Thus, he became known as Ghaṭa-udkaca. Ghaṭa-udkaca was devoted to the Pāṇḍavas. He became their beloved, always self-existent. During the time of residence, he spoke to them. Hidiṁbā, having made the time, returned to her own path. Ghaṭa-udkaca, the best of demons, said, "I will approach my father." The slaughter of the crane.

English: This is known to me beforehand, O best of the Bharatas, how those residing in the city of Dhṛtarāṣṭra are situated in unrighteousness. Having understood this, I have come to seek the highest good; there should be no sorrow here; all this is for your happiness. If all of you are indeed with me, the relatives will speak with humility and like children. Therefore, I am currently more than you; I will seek your welfare, so understand this. This city is beautiful and free from ailments; it is hidden for those who long for my arrival. Thus, Vyāsa consoled them, and having reached the one wheel, he comforted Kuntī. This son of yours is the son of Dharma, Yudhishthira; he will rule the earth along with the kings. Having conquered the entire earth through righteousness, Bhīma will surely bring about the destruction of the unrighteous. Your sons and the mighty charioteers will enjoy happiness in their own kingdom. And the tiger among men will conquer this earth, with the Rajasuya and Ashvamedha sacrifices as their duties.

English: 568 Bakavadhapava Then, O lord of the world, they became like the city dwellers with their own qualities. They used to offer food to Kuntī, always without hesitation. She divided the portions, and they ate separately. Thus, the heroes, O Parantapa, were in distress. Bhīma, the great warrior, was in his own abode. At that time, the great time passed over the noble king of the Bharata lineage. Then, at some point, the Bharatas went to the forest, and Bhīma was there with them. Then, Kuntī heard a great sound of lamentation from outside. Seeing them weeping, she was filled with compassion and could not bear it, O king. Pṛthā, in great sorrow, spoke to Bhīma, who was endowed with mercy. "We are living happily in the abode of the Brahmana, unknown to others, and we are honored." She always thought, "What can I do for my son, the Brahmana, to ensure that he lives happily in the house?"

English: Thus, the man has done this, in which ALA. As much as the evil-doers of this, more than that. This is the suffering of the Brāhmaṇa that has befallen. If there is help for him there, may it be a good deed. Bhīma said: Let this suffering be known, from where it has arisen. I will act accordingly, even if it is very difficult. Vērāmpāyana said: Thus, while speaking, they heard the sound of the great sage. The assembly of that Brāhmaṇa was indeed very great. Then, Kuntī quickly entered the inner quarters of that great soul. There, she saw the Brāhmaṇa along with Bhāryā and the son, and the granddaughter also, with a distorted face. The Brāhmaṇa said: Alas, this life is indeed worthless, devoid of essence. The root of suffering is dependence, and it is dear to the foolish. In life, there is the greatest suffering; in life, there is the greatest fever. In the life of the present, SSAA Ya: Even if one is single-minded, he does not enjoy desire.

English: These separations are considered the greatest suffering. Some say that the highest liberation does not exist at all, and hell is indeed attainable. The greater suffering arises from the separation of those who are dear. I do not see a means by which I can be freed from this calamity, whether through sons or wives. I have previously strived, as you know, O Brāhmaṇi, to reach that peace, but I have not heard from you. Here I have grown, and my father is here as well. Indeed, my father is old, and my mother is also here for a long time; what joy is there in living there with relatives who have passed away? This is your desire, O friend, and my words are not heard. The loss of relatives has come, bringing great sorrow. Or perhaps this is my fate; I do not see any way to abandon my relatives while living, cruelly. I have a gentle and devoted companion, like a mother, always. A friend appointed by the gods, always leading to the highest destination. A home is established by mother and father, always a part of domestic life; having chosen rightly, one should live according to dharma. The killing of the duck.

English: I cannot abandon my mother, who is endowed with the wealth of a home and is virtuous and unharmful for the sake of life. I cannot abandon my sister, who is always devoted. How can I abandon my daughter? I am not capable of doing so, having not attained the age of maturity. The great soul has entrusted the deposit of the child. In her, the granddaughters are lamenting along with their fathers. How can I abandon her, whom I have myself produced? Some think that the father is more important than the daughter, but I do not consider either of them equal to my own. In the womb, the birth is established, and thus I cannot abandon the innocent child. Even if I were to abandon myself, I would not be able to live without her. This abandonment of any of them is cruel and blameworthy. If I abandon myself, they will perish without me. I am indeed in a difficult situation and unable to escape this calamity. Alas, I will go to you, accompanied by all my relatives. It is better to die with all than to live alone.

English: The Brahmin said: There should be no distress for you at any time, as this is not the time for distress. Indeed, this time of distress does not exist for you. All humans must eventually face death. The distress that arises from the lower nature does not exist here. A son or daughter will surely be lost to you. Your wealth and righteousness are indeed visible here. As you desire, so it will be for you; you have received it from me. The daughter and the son have been made by you, and I am indebted to you. Considering all this, you should abandon the self and the blame; save yourself and this child. Thus addressed by her, he, weeping slowly, released his tears in the assembly.

Let me also be heard, and let something be done after listening. 002 I, indeed, am to be abandoned; there is no doubt about this in your youth. Abandoning me, you should save all with me alone. 003 Thus, it is said that the offspring will save me; when that time arrives, I will be like a shadow. 007 Here or there, may he save me; or may he save me in every way; the son is called a son. 005 In the end, even the grandfathers will always protect the grandchildren; they themselves will save the life of the father. 006 This younger brother of mine has gone to the other world; Soon, he will not return. 007 When the father departs to heaven and is destroyed, my brother will surely be separated from the ancestors; that will be unpleasant for them. 008 Abandoned by the father and also by the mother, I have no doubt about the night. 009 When you are freed from illness, my mother and brother will be my refuge; the offspring and the offering will surely be established. 010 The soul, the son, the friend, and the daughter are indeed in difficulty.

English: PIAA, unite with me in righteousness. O helpless, miserable girl, wandering here and there, I will be without you, alas, dear father. Now I will undertake the liberation of this family, I will create a difficult task. Or if you go there, abandoning me, O best of the twice-born, I will be afflicted, please consider me too. For our sake, O best one, for the sake of the righteous, Protect yourself, abandon me. Do not let time pass by, With the water you have given, may it be well for me. What greater sorrow can there be than that we are together? Those who are asking, let us run like the wind. When you are free from suffering, I will be in happiness. Thus, she is greatly distressed, Her father and mother, and she, the girl. Then, having released the weeping ones, the son of them, With tear-filled eyes, raised his arms, clearly expressing his sorrow. Do not weep, father, do not weep, mother, do not weep, sister, he said, Smiling, all of them, he also spoke.

English: The city and the land are protected by the forces of demons; for this reason, we have no fear from the beings. The salary for that is fixed, the food of the Shālīvāha; a bull and a man, whoever takes that, goes. Each man takes his share of the food; he who is fortunate becomes blessed with many years. For the liberation of those who strive, the demons devour those who have sons and wives. In the royal house, the king is not established in this way; may there be no affliction for the people, so that today may be eternal. Indeed, we are surely residing in the realm of the weak; always striving for the king, we are dependent. Whose words are to be spoken by the brāhmaṇas, or by the chandas followers? Indeed, they will be fulfilled like the desires of birds. The king should first be found, then fear, then wealth; in the accumulation of three, he should support his relatives and sons. If this trio is opposed by me, we shall endure this calamity. This is the one who has come to us, the destroyer of the hut; the food of a single man should be given, the salary by me. And I do not have wealth for any man.

English: I will not abandon my own self or my son for the sake of others. However, I believe that it is better to know the truth about my own self. There is no sin in killing for the sake of Brahman, nor is there any sin in killing oneself. I do not desire to kill myself, nor do I see any sin in killing for the sake of others. In the case of killing a Brahmin, I do not see any redemption, nor do I see it as cruel or trivial. Abandoning a home is not cruel, nor is killing someone who seeks refuge. The wise do not consider it cruel to kill in times of distress. I do not consider the killing of a Brahmin as something I would ever approve of. Kuntī said: This is my firm resolve, that my son should be protected. My son cannot be a demon, for he is strong, virtuous, and radiant.

English: The one who was seated in the assembly then asked his mother. What does Bhīma intend to do? Is he going to act with strength? Is he indeed willing to do this? Kuntī said: By my word, the one who is a great warrior will act. Yudhishthira said: What is this sharp act done by you, O wicked one? Indeed, the righteous do not praise the abandonment of a son. How can you wish to abandon your own son for the sake of another's son? This act is contrary to the conduct of the world. By whom do we all find comfort, relying on his arms? We shall again seek the kingdom that has been taken away. The one who is thinking of the valor of Duryodhana does not sleep, suffering along with the crow. By the valor of that hero, the one who was killed in the house of the dice is freed from sins. By relying on the valor of that hero, we consider this land of plenty as ours, having defeated the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra. What is your decision regarding this abandonment?

English: Is your mind not troubled, O AGA, by the pain? Kuntī said: O Yudhishthira, there is no sorrow regarding Vṛkodara; nor has this decision been made by me due to weakness of mind. Here, we, the sons of the brāhmaṇa, are comfortably situated; this response, O father, has been carefully considered by me. Such is the extent of a man’s actions that it does not perish. I have seen Bhīma’s valor then in the great house of Jatā; my trust in Vṛkodara is due to the killing of Hidimba. Then, indeed, Bhīma is as great as a thousand serpents; by whom you all are like elephants in the presence of the king of elephants. There is no one as strong as Vṛkodara; none has been, nor will be, who can match even the mighty Vajradhara himself. As soon as he was born, he fell from my lap onto the mountain; the stone of that great weight was indeed crushed. Then, remembering the strength of Bhīma, O Pāṇḍava, I resolved to take action against the brāhmaṇa. This is not determined by greed, ignorance, or delusion; but my decision regarding the strength of Bhīma has been made with wisdom. Then, both of us will be fulfilled, O Yudhishthira, in the future. The killing of the crane.

English: The remedy and the great conduct of virtue. A Kṣatriya should assist a Brāhmaṇa in any matter of importance; thus it is heard. A Kṣatriya, being a Kṣatriya, should not kill another Kṣatriya; he attains great fame in this world and the next. A Kṣatriya who assists a courtesan in battle delights all beings in the world. A king who liberates a Śūdra seeking refuge attains a birth in a noble family due to royal merit. Thus, the Lord Vyāsa, the son of Kuru, spoke this ancient wisdom, which was greatly desired. Yudhiṣṭhira said: This is indeed fitting, O mother, as it has been done for the distressed Brāhmaṇa. This Bhīma will surely return after killing the man-eater. Just as the city-dwellers do not find this, so this Brāhmaṇa should be spoken of.

English: Bhīma spoke. Then, during the night, the Pāṇḍava took food, and Bhīma went there where the man-eater was. Upon reaching the forest, the powerful Pāṇḍava called out the name of that food. Then, hearing Bhīma's words, the man-eater came, well-prepared, where Bhīma was situated. The giant, with great speed, seemed to tear the earth apart, making a fierce expression with his three peaks and baring his teeth. Seeing Bhīma, the man-eater, with eyes wide open, spoke this word. "Who is this food prepared for my purpose? This is a meal for my foolishness." Hearing this, Bhīma laughed, disregarding the man-eater, and was very eager. Then, making a fearsome sound, the man-eater rushed at Bhīma, intent on killing him. Yet, not paying attention to him, the mighty Bhīma, the Pāṇḍava, devoured the food, slayer of other heroes. With anger, the man-eater of Kuntī's son approached. The slaying of Baka.

English: He struck the back with both hands while standing behind. Thus, the mighty Bhīma, struck by the hands, did not look at the demon. Then, that demon, being enraged, took a tree and prepared to strike Bhīma again. Then Bhīma, having eaten slowly, the man among men, touched the food and stood joyful in battle, the mighty one. He seized that tree with great strength. With his left hand, Bhīma, smiling, O Bhārata. Then he again, having lifted many kinds of trees, hurled them at Bhīma, the son of Pāṇḍu. A fierce battle arose, O great king, between Baka and the Pāṇḍava. Having called out loudly, Baka seized the mighty Bhīmasena with his arms. Even Bhīmasena, embracing that demon with his great arms, was seen to be bursting forth with great speed. Being seized by Bhīma and also by the Pāṇḍava, they fought fiercely like two powerful men. With their great speed, the earth trembled, and the great trees were shaken at that time.

English: From that time, the demons were seen there, O Bhārata, by the inhabitants of the city. Then Bhīma, taking the man who had fallen, placed him in the doorway and went away unnoticed. Then Bhīma, having killed him, went to the place and reported to the king as it happened. Then the men, emerging from the city, saw the demon lying dead, drenched in blood. That terrifying place, filled with the dead bodies, was reached by a single wheel. Then a thousand men of the city came there, along with the aged and young women. Then all were astonished, seeing that exceedingly powerful being, like a god. Then they began to count whose turn it was today for the feast, and knowing this, they asked that brāhmaṇa. Thus questioned repeatedly, while protecting the Pāṇḍavas, he spoke to all the citizens. A certain brāhmaṇa, knowing my command, wept with his relatives.

English: The learned Brahmana, having performed the proper rituals, approached the external Brahman. Then, the Pandavas, along with Kunti, gathered around the Brahmana, listening to his stories. He narrated various tales about different regions and the diverse kings and their ancient histories. There, Janamejaya asked about the extraordinary wedding of Yajñasena, which took place in Panchala. Hearing about the wondrous deeds of Krishna, they inquired in detail about the story of that great soul. How did Krishna come into being from the fire? How did Drona, the great archer, teach all the Kauravas? How did the dear friend become different, and for whose sake? Thus prompted by them, the Brahmana narrated everything about the birth of Draupadi.

English: Chaitrarathapavana Brāhmaṇa said: At the Ganges' entrance, a great sage named Mahābabhūva appeared, a wise one among the Bharadwajas, always engaged in rituals. He went to anoint the Ganges, who had come there as a pure woman. There, the sage, with a clarified butter offering, spoke by the riverbank. At that time, the wind was blowing, and he was wearing a garment that was pulled down. In that place, the mind of the young men was attached, and the joyful one was engaged in the act of procreation. Then, there arose Drona, the son of that wise one, who studied the Vedas. The friend of Bharadwaja was a king named Pṛṣata, and from him, there was also a son named Drupada. He regularly went to the hermitage and played and studied with Drona, the best of the Kṣatriyas. Then, after Pṛṣata had passed, King Drupada arose.

English: Drona also heard Rama desiring wealth. When Rama had entered the forest, the son of Bharadwaja spoke. Know that Drona has come to me, desiring wealth. Rama said: This has been rejected by me. Choose either weapons or body, O Brahman, not the other. Drona said: If weapons, then all of them, and also the destruction of them. To give the use of all of them is indeed great for you. The Brahman said: Thus spoken, then the son of Bhrigu gave to him. Receiving it, Drona became accomplished then. Having been struck and also approved by Rama, Having reached the great one, he became superior among men. Then, having reached Drupada, the mighty son of Bharadwaja, Know that the man-tiger is my friend. Drupada said: The non-Brahman is not a friend of the Brahman, nor is the charioteer a friend of the charioteer. What will remain of friendship even among kings and landowners?

English: The Brahmana said: Having determined in his mind, he went to the city of the Kurus, aided by the serpent. Taking various riches from there, Bhīṣma gave them to the wise Droṇa upon his arrival. Droṇa then spoke this entire statement to all his disciples. The teacher's salary indeed fluctuates; it should be spoken of by the sinless. When all the Pāṇḍavas were exhausted and had completed their tasks, then Droṇa spoke this word regarding the salary. There is a king named Drupada in the city of Chhatravati; let that kingdom be quickly given to me. Then the sons of Pāṇḍu, having defeated Drupada in battle, were bound to Droṇa along with his minister. Droṇa said: I request you, O king, to befriend me again; for a king is indeed not a friend to a king. Thus, I have exerted myself in the kingdom; I am on the southern side of the Yajñasena, and I am on the northern side of the Bhāgirathi.

English: The Brāhmaṇa said: The great one, though unworthy, did not depart from the heart of the king; he became emaciated due to his troubled mind. King Drupada, who was without anger, sought the Brāhmaṇas for assistance, desiring a son, afflicted in mind by grief. He constantly thought, "There is no one superior to my offspring." Having given birth to sons, he felt detachment, thinking, "Alas, they are bound," and he sighed deeply, wishing to confront Droṇa. He contemplated Droṇa's influence, humility, and deeds, and with strength and valor, he did not yield. The best of kings, striving to respond, was surrounded by the impure. The king arrived at the sacred abode of the Brāhmaṇas, where no one was unclean, and there was no one who was not a Brahmin, nor was there anyone who had taken a vow of renunciation.

English: The one who sees the fruit does not measure the faults of those connected to it; he who distinguishes does not grieve, how can he be elsewhere? The one who studies the scriptures and resides in the guru's abode, always consumes the remnants of others. The one who is skilled in the qualities of food, O Agni, repeatedly. I consider you, O brother, as one who seeks the fruit; go to him, O king, he will offer you a sacrifice. While contemplating this, the king, feeling disgusted, heard the words of the messenger and became agitated. Having worshipped the worthy sage, he spoke to him. O Lord, you should give me eight thousand cows; you are worthy to fulfill the desires of Drona and others. He is indeed the best among the knower of Brahman and the best among cereals; he will defeat me in battle. There is no Kṣatriya equal to him on this earth, the chief among the Kurus, the wise Bharadvāja. Drona's arrows are capable of taking away the lives of beings; his bow is unmatched and great. He, with the speed of an external arrow, protects the Kṣatriya; the great-minded Bharadvāja opposes the mighty warriors.

English: For the destruction of the Kṣatriyas, he is established like Jamadagni. For him, O king, there is a terrible and unconquerable force. The Brāhmaṇa, like a fire that consumes offerings, radiates brilliance. Thus, he firmly holds the Kṣatra, the foremost of the Brāhmaṇas. In the established Brahman-Kṣatriya, the external radiance diminishes. I am dependent on the Kṣatriya's strength, like a bird that has fallen. Having approached the distinguished Droṇa, I will invoke you, O possessor of Brahman wealth. I will strike down Droṇa's son in battle. What should I do for you, O Yāja, to obtain the wealth of cows? Thus instructed, the Yāja prepared for the sacrifice. He also urged the Guru, desiring to perform the sacrifice. The Yāja vowed to destroy Droṇa, and he did so. Then, the great ascetic Yāja, the king, revealed the means for the son to prosper. That son is of great valor, great brilliance, and great strength. O king, you will have a son like him. The king, having surrounded the slayer of Bhāradvāja, performed the action for the success of the task. At the end of the sacrifice, the Yāja invoked the goddess, saying, "O queen, I am here, with you present as a pair."

English: The goddess said: "O Brahman, I bear the auspicious scents; I am obstructed by the son; remain, O my beloved, for the sake of the son." Yāja said: "By the sacrifice, the offering is prepared; by the offering, it is made pure. How can you not be present, O learned one, whether you stand or not?" The Brāhmaṇa said: "Thus addressed by Yāja, the offering was made, and from the fire, a boy resembling a deity emerged." "With a fiery hue, a terrible form, wearing a crown, holding a bow, he roared repeatedly." "He ascended the chariot, and then he proceeded." "Then they proclaimed: 'Be auspicious, be auspicious!'" "The prince, the remover of fear, the bringer of fame to the Pāñcālas, is born to slay Droṇa." Thus spoke the great being, the celestial one, at that time. And the maiden, also a Pāñcālī, arose from the altar, beautiful, charming, and delightful. With a lotus-like face, she appeared as a divine being, taking on a human form.

English: The fragrance of the blue lotus, whose essence is like that, which possesses a supreme form, unmatched in the world. She, born with a beautiful body, speaks with eloquence, the dark one, desiring the destruction of the Kṣatriyas. This beautiful one will accomplish the work of the gods; for this reason, great fear will arise among the Kṣatriyas. Hearing this, all the Pāñcālas roared like a lion's pride. And the earth could not bear the weight of these lions. Then the strong one, the daughter of the sage, approached them, and no one could recognize her as another's mother. Thus spoke the sage to her, wishing to please the king; and their names became renowned, filling the hearts of all. Due to their boldness and extreme desire, this young prince will become the master of the earth. Only Krishna, calling out to Krishna, thus the couple was born at the great sacrifice of Drupada. Then the powerful Bharadvāja brought the Pāñcāla to his own abode. The wise one, considering the divine, performed the protection of Drona.

English: Vyāsa said: Hearing this, the sons of Kuntī became like those pierced by Shalya. All the great charioteers became of disturbed minds. Then Kuntī, seeing her sons bewildered and lost in thought, spoke this word to Yudhishthira, the truth-teller. Having stayed for a long time in the abode of the Brahmana, enjoying in the beautiful city, O Yudhishthira, The beautiful forests and groves that are here, all those have been seen again and again. Again, those very ones please us, not so for us. O hero, the Kurunandana is not so. We shall go there, if you think it right, O father. The delightful sight will be there. The Panchalas are indeed heard to be prosperous. The king Yajñasena is said to be a Brahmana. Staying in one place for a long time is indeed not my opinion. If you think so, O son, we shall go there.

English: The worship of you, O Brāhmaṇas, is not given to those worthy of worship. Then, having spoken thus, the Lord Rishi said: "These stories are indeed wonderful." There was a girl of great virtue, the daughter of the sage Kācira, endowed with excellent qualities. By her own actions, she became unfortunate; the beautiful and chaste girl did not attain a husband. Having undergone austerities, she was unhappy with her husband; through her penance, she pleased Śaṅkara with a sharp thorn. The Lord, being pleased with her, spoke to the ascetic woman: "O beautiful one, I grant you a boon." Then the Lord spoke: "I wish for a husband endowed with all good qualities." He, the Lord, replied to her: "Five husbands will be yours, O auspicious one." "Grant me one husband who will be the best among them," said Śaṅkara. "You have been told to have five husbands; I again say that this will happen as stated." The girl, who has gone to the abode of the gods, is the wife of the divine form; she is designated as the wife of Kṛṣṇa, the unblemished one.

English: This text appears to be a collection of verses or snippets from a larger work, possibly related to mythology or philosophy. Here are the translations: 1. "The fierce bowman spoke this word." 2. "The terrifying twilight that comes at the end of the night is called by those who are in distress." 3. "The conduct of the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas is known here as the conduct of humans." 4. "Those who are greedy and act in those moments are captured along with the foolish Rākṣasas." 5. "Then the wise people take the hair of Val Aya, capturing all men, even those of great strength." 6. "Do not approach me, stay away; why do you not recognize me, having obtained the waters of Bhāgirathī?" 7. "The Gandharva of the burning leaves, I am indeed a friend of Kubera, honored and respected." 8. "This forest is known as Aṅgārapaṇa; I will dwell there with my words and desires." 9. "Neither the lowly nor the gods nor humans approach this; they take an oath together." 10. "Ajana spoke: 'In the sea, beyond the Himalayas, who is the one that takes possession at night?'"

English: We are also endowed with power; we do not forsake you in times of distress. Indeed, humans seek you in moments of crisis. Once, from the Himalayas, the essence of gold was released. It reaches the ocean, dividing into seven streams. Becoming pure and celestial, this one, having attained the divine fragrance, brings forth unparalleled joy. Thus, the Ganges, difficult to cross due to sinful deeds, becomes fragrant like the divine, as if untainted by sin. The divine river, unbound and auspicious, how do you wish to be that eternal one? How can we, unbound by your words, not attain the sacred waters of Bhāgirathī as desired? Veraṁpāyana said: Hearing the words of the ignorant, angered, he released the arrows, like venomous snakes. The Pandava, spinning the wheel, released arrows, and all were struck by Dhananjaya. Ajana said: The fragrance of the divine is not used in the fearful; it is like foam, dissipating.

English: Who indeed would kill the enemy, O Ripu-sūdana? Arjuna said: Having taken this, go to Gandharva, do not grieve. Today, the king of the Kurus, Yudhishthira, assures you of safety. The Gandharva said: I have conquered, I release the name Pūvaka. Neither by strength nor by the assembly of people. Having obtained this, I, who am the divine bearer, Wish to fight with the Gandharva by the power of my age. This is indeed a strange milk, my excellent chariot. Thus, having become a colorful chariot, I became a burnt chariot. This knowledge was indeed gathered by me through austerity. Today, I will present it to that great soul who gives life. For one who has come seeking refuge, If one connects the life with the enemy, what good is it? This knowledge is called "eyes," it gives the mind to the moon. He gave to me, the universal being, the universal being gave. This one, having reached the coward, the teacher's gift is lost. The arrival of this was spoken by me, understand the valor. If one wishes to see, let him see something in the worlds. Chariot of the colorful chariot.

English: The one who is eager to cut the bond of desire. In the same position, I will impart knowledge for six months. By this knowledge, O King, the lineage of men is purified. I, the best of men, am the giver of a hundred to your five brothers. The divine Gandharvas, with their heavenly fragrances, become diminished; they do not give wealth secretly. Previously done by Mahendra in the slaying of Vritra, it is fragmented in hundreds and thousands. Then, the portion of the god is worshipped, whatever means is remembered in the world. The one with a boon in hand is remembered as a Kṣatriya. The courtesans and demons are of the lowest kind. The speech of the Kṣatriya is remembered as that of a horseman. The charioteer and the horses are born from the chariot. Those who are desirous and swift in desire are present; these Gandharvas will fulfill desires with their horses. Ajana spoke.

English: Fee Teal: The stories of the Kurus are told in detail by them. I have heard from Narada and other divine beings about the qualities of your wise ancestors, O hero. I have also seen the ocean of the earth, the influence of your family, Vasu. I know the excellence in archery in the Vedas, and I am aware of the renowned Bharadvāja in the three worlds. I know Dharma, Vāyu, Indra, and the Ashvins, as well as Pandu and the six noble ones of the Kuru lineage. I am the path for the ancestors, the divine and human beings. The divine souls, the great souls, the best among all families, all of you brothers are heroes with good conduct. However, the excellent intellect of you who are devoted souls is known to me, even though I have made a path for you here. A man cannot bear the great burden of the self, relying on the wealth of others. By night, our strength increases even more, for from that, O Kaunteya, anger has always arisen in me. I am defeated by you in battle, O son of Kunti, and by that very means, I instruct you, listen to me.

English: Brahmacarya is the highest dharma, and you are also bound by it. Therefore, I, having been defeated by you in this battle, will follow the path. He who is a Kṣatriya and indulges in desires, does not live at all if he fights at night. Even if a king indulges in desires, he will perish in battle if he does not win at night. Therefore, whatever is desired by the king, let it be sought after. The priests should be composed and self-controlled. Those who are devoted to the Vedas, pure and truthful, will be the priests of kings. Victory is assured for the king who is disciplined, and he will have no rival. To gain what is unattainable, and to protect what has been gained, the king should appoint a priest endowed with virtues. The king should stand firm in the opinion of the priest if he wishes to rule the earth. Having attained the best of mountains, the ocean of ambrosia from all sides. A Brahmin cannot conquer a king merely by lineage or by birth. Therefore, understand this: by the lineage of the Kurus, the kingdom can be ruled for a long time with the Brahmin at the forefront.

English: As the sun shines brightly in the sky, so did the king of the earth, the one who gives light, become radiant. As the Brahmavādins praise the rising sun, so did the people, who were external and unrestrained, praise Partha. Due to the brilliance of the moon, the king, who was dear and radiant like the sun, became a ruler of the friends. Thus, the king, who was of noble conduct, thought to give to him, the one who was self-illuminating. At one time, the king, the illustrious and renowned one, roamed the forest in search of game. While hunting, he was afflicted by hunger and thirst, and the horse of the king, like a mountain, fell. The king, having seen the horse that had died on the path, beheld a maiden with beautiful eyes. He saw a maiden, whose beauty was like that of a lotus. The king, captivated by her form, again became enamored by her radiance. In the mountain abode, she, with her lovely eyes, stood, and she appeared like a golden deer among the trees. And she, with her body full of life, was indeed enchanting.

English: The king perceived the fruit of his eyes. From birth, whatever the king saw, there was nothing like that form. Bound by that gaze, he did not move, neither in the country nor anywhere else. Surely, this form was created by the creator, mixing divine and human qualities. Thus, he began to contemplate the wealth of beauty. In the world, the king was then restrained. The king, seeing that auspicious sight, was troubled in mind, tormented by desire. Burning intensely, he spoke to the illustrious woman. "Who are you, daughter of Rambha, and why do you stand here? How do you wander alone in the forest, with a pure smile?" You are indeed adorned with all ornaments, like the desired ornament among these ornaments. I do not consider you a goddess, nor a demoness, nor a yakṣī, nor a rākṣasī, nor a woman of enjoyment, nor a celestial nymph, nor a human. Among the beautiful maidens I have seen, I do not think any are like you, O you who intoxicates the mind.

English: Thus addressed by the king with sweet words, she stood before him with a broad waist. Then the king, with dark feet, spoke to her with a mind filled with desire and a voice that was uncertain. "Please, O dark-footed one, worship me, for my life is indeed dependent on you." "For your sake, O wide-eyed one, I am pierced by the arrows of desire, and it calms down only when I see you." "Consumed by the great desire, you, with your full and beautiful hips, are the one who brings auspiciousness." "My life is indeed dependent on you; what can I do, O beautiful one, who speaks like a man?" "I cannot live for myself, so, O wide-eyed one, please show me compassion." "Do not abandon me, O dark-footed one, for you can indeed save me through your love." "O timid one, through the Gandharva marriage, unite with me, for among marriages, the Gandharva is considered the best." Tapati spoke: "I am not the one, O king, who can marry without my father's consent."

English: 620 Chaitrarathapavana The minister, accompanied by his retinue, saw him in the great forest, fallen to the ground like the flag of Indra. Indeed, he was a great archer, fallen to the earth, devoid of horses; he became like a blazing fire to his minister. With urgency, he approached, bewildered by affection, and lifted the king, who was enchanted by desire. Like a father lifting his fallen son from the ground, he, aged in wisdom and years, did so with great effort. The minister, having lifted him, became free from fever and spoke to him with auspicious words, awakened from his stupor. "Do not fear, O son of Bhima; may you be blessed, O sinless one." Exhausted from thirst and fatigue, he lifted the king, who had fallen in battle on the battlefield. With cool water, the lord of the waters bathed him, touching not the crown of the king with the fragrant lotus. Then, having regained his life, he released everything, except for that one minister. Then, by the king's command, he stood in opposition; the king, however, reappeared on the mountain. Then, having become pure in that mountain, with folded hands, he prayed to the sun, standing with the earth beneath his arms.

English: He is indeed the king, endowed with great wisdom and noble qualities; he is capable of restraining the birds of your desires. The Gandharva spoke. Thus addressed, the Sun, having determined to give, replied to the Brahmin. O king, you are the best among the sages; what else can be said about the best of women? The one who is the best among women, the Sun himself, gave to Vasiṣṭha, the great sage. Then the great sage accepted that maiden, Tapati. Vasiṣṭha, having been released, again came back to the place where the renowned Kīṭi became the chief of the Kurus. That king, with his mind absorbed in love, saw the beautiful smiling daughter of the gods, Tapati. With Vasiṣṭha as his companion, he was exceedingly joyful. After twelve nights of difficulty, the pure-souled sage Vasiṣṭha, the divine sage, arrived. The one who is worshipped through austerities, the bestower of boons, the lord of the cows, is indeed Vasiṣṭha, shining with brilliance.

English: Thus, the noble man, having been duly authorized by Vasiṣṭha, desired to conquer the city along with his wife. Then, in that city, the king enjoyed with his wife for twelve years in forests and waters. In that city of the king, there were twelve sons, and the thousand-eyed one did not prevail over them. Then, afflicted by hunger, the man became like a corpse, and the city of that king was enveloped as if by death. Then, having seen such a sight, the great sage Vasiṣṭha, with a warm heart, approached the best of kings. He brought him to that city, where he had lived with his wife for many years. Then, when the rain came, the king's messenger entered the city again. Then, the entire kingdom rejoiced, and the city was filled with great joy.

English: There was a sage, O Lord, who spoke this. The Gandharva said: Conquered by austerity, always victorious over the immortal. Whose feet are borne by both desire and anger. He who does not cut off the noble-minded of the Kausikas, Holding the great wrath due to the offense against Viśvāmitra. The powerful lord, afflicted by the misfortune of his son, Did not consider anything dreadful without Viśvāmitra. He who, having been struck down by death, Did not move like the ocean at high tide. Having attained him, the great-souled, the kings of Ikṣvāku, Ruled over this earth. Having obtained the foremost of priests, the great sage Vasiṣṭha, The kings, O son of Kuru, worshipped him with various offerings. He indeed defeated all those noble kings, Like Brahma, the best of the Pandavas, like Brihaspati among the immortals. Therefore, the one whose soul is devoted to dharma, desiring knowledge of the Vedic dharma, Let some virtuous Brahmana be sought. For a Kshatriya born to desire to rule the earth, The former priest is to be engaged for the increase of the kingdom.

English: Vasiṣṭha, the foremost sage, having regarded the arrival, honored Viśvāmitra, the best among men, with worship. With water for washing the feet and a welcoming gesture, he also honored him with wild offerings. Then, the great-souled Vasiṣṭha, who is like a wish-fulfilling cow, spoke, "May you grant your desires," and thus she began to milk the desires. From the village, the herbs and the milk flowed, and the nectar-like essence, the supreme elixir, was produced. Various edible items and drinks, as well as delightful ambrosial preparations, were offered. The king, honored by these desires, was greatly pleased, along with his ministers and strong allies. With six spacious sides, surrounded by five, having the eyes of a frog, and with a form that is not to be criticized, He beheld the beautiful Shankhakaṇā, with a robust neck and a charming appearance, and was astonished. Vasiṣṭha's milk-giving Nandī was praised by him, and Viśvāmitra, being very pleased, then spoke to the sage. "By the power of my kingdom or by the grace of the cows, grant me Nandini, O great sage." Vasiṣṭha spoke.

English: Devatātithi, Pitr, and the milk-giving Nandini, I do not wish to give you, O sinless one, even with my kingdom. Viśvāmitra said: I am a Kṣatriya, O Bhavānī, a practitioner of austerities and study. What valor is there among the Brāhmaṇas, who are peaceful and self-controlled? O Abudena, you do not give me what I desire. I will not abandon my duty; I will lead your cow by force. Vasiṣṭha said: You are indeed a king, and a Kṣatriya of great strength. Do as you wish quickly; do not deliberate. The Gandharva said: Thus addressed, Viśvāmitra forcibly took the cow Nandini, which shone like the moon among swans. Struck by the staff, she was being driven away, and the beautiful Nandini, trembling, was then with Vasiṣṭha. Approaching, she stood facing the path, her divine form turned towards the Lord, and even though she was being driven away, she did not leave the hermitage. Vasiṣṭha said: I hear your cries, O auspicious one; they are repeated by the one who is crying.

English: By force, I am indeed Nandi, capable of enduring. The Gandharva spoke: But she, from their strength, Nandi, the best of Bharata, Fearing Viśvāmitra, approached Vasiṣṭha. The cow spoke: Struck by the stone staff, crying out, I, without a protector, O Viśvāmitra, why do you ignore me? The Gandharva spoke: Thus, at that time, on the path, the great sage, Did not stir, nor did he move, steadfast in his vow. Vasiṣṭha spoke: Among Kṣatriyas, strength is the best, among Brāhmaṇas, endurance is the strength. If endurance pleases me, then let it be delightful. The cow spoke: What, O Lord, do you say, that I have abandoned you? I have been abandoned by you, and cannot be led away by force. Vasiṣṭha spoke: I do not abandon you, O auspicious one, stay if possible. Thus, bound, my dear one, you are.

English: Gandharva spoke. Hearing this, the daughter of Vasiṣṭha, the one with the flowing waters, Kr̥odhara, with red eyes, made the army of Viśvāmitra flee completely. Then, Kālī, being angry, like the sun, with a blazing form, released a great weapon. Asujat, the powerful one, with a tail like a lion, also released a stream of anger towards the Yavanas. The Pundarikas, Kirātas, Dramiḍas, and Singhalas, and also the Dardas, were thus affected. Then, the great army was released, with various divisions and many armed warriors. Surrounded by the enraged Viśvāmitra, one warrior stood alone, surrounded by five or seven. With a great weapon, the mighty Kālī then released a banyan tree. Seeing this, all were terrified of Viśvāmitra.

English: He approached them. While they were discussing thus, the sage Viśvāmitra, the powerful one, came near. Then the best of kings, having understood the sage, recognized him as the son of Vasiṣṭha, like Vasiṣṭha himself in brilliance. Then Viśvāmitra, having understood his own self, also desired to approach them, wishing for his own dear one. But then, cursed by him, the best of kings, went to the powerful one for refuge, wishing to please him. Understanding his mood, the son of the Kurus, Viśvāmitra then ordered protection for the king. By the curse of that one and by the command of Viśvāmitra, a demon named Kiṅkara then entered the king. Then, knowing that he was seized by the demon, the sage Viśvāmitra also withdrew from that place. Then the king, knowing himself, though being oppressed by the powerful demon, remained firm. A certain brāhmaṇa saw him, the king, who was again set out, and asked him for food, being hungry. Then the king spoke to the brāhmaṇa, his friend, "Be at ease, O brāhmaṇa, I will give you food as you desire."

But the king, possessed by a demon, said to the Sūta, "Go and feed him with human flesh." Thus instructed, the Sūta, going to the place of execution, quickly seized human flesh, trembling. Having prepared it properly, he placed it before the Brahmana. To him, the Brahmana, the ascetic, gave food. The best of the twice-born, with keen sight, said, "This food is not to be eaten." English: The curse of the powerful one was pronounced upon the king who had killed the double. Possessed by the strength of the demons, he then fell unconscious. Then, the best of kings, deprived of his senses by the demon, spoke to that Shakti, looking like a tiger, O Bharata, without delay. Since this curse, which is not good, has been cast upon you by me, I shall begin to devour humans. Thus speaking, he immediately seized him as if he were a life, and the tiger began to consume Shakti, as if he were a desired prey. But the red one was killed, and then Viśvāmitra again commanded that demon, just like the son of Vasiṣṭha. He began to devour the sons of the great Vasiṣṭha, just like a lion devours small animals. Hearing that his sons had been killed by Viśvāmitra, Vasiṣṭha bore that grief like a great mountain bears the earth. He devised a plan for self-destruction, that best of sages. The best among the wise did not think that the destruction of the Kurus was good. The Lord Rishi released himself from the peak of Meru, and his head fell upon the stone like a heap of cotton. He did not die from the fall when the Pandava was struck; then the Lord entered the great forest.

English: The great sage, released from the noose, then rose up. He named the river as Mahānṛṣi. Then, in grief, he reflected and did not remain in one place. He went to the rivers and lakes. Then he again searched for the river Hemavatī, which was under the influence of the fierce demon. Considering him equal to fire, the river bank thought of him and thus became known as Didirūtā. Then, having settled on the ground, he could not bear to be without himself and thus went back to the hermitage. Following the invisible woman, he approached the hermitage and then heard the sound of Vedic recitation. On the back, there were six decorated pillars. "Who is following me?" he said. "I am known by the name of the unseen," replied the sage. Mahābhāga, endowed with austerity, spoke. "O daughter, whose is the sound of Vedic recitation? Long ago, I heard it as if from the power of the Vedas." They spoke.

English: This Fel has arisen from your son, O powerful one. He is equal to twelve here, having studied the Vedas, O sage. The Gandharva spoke: Thus addressed, Vasiṣṭha, the foremost sage, became joyful. He said that there is a lineage, and then he turned away from death. Then, having returned, he, along with that wife, approached Kalmaṣapāda, who was seated in the solitary forest. The king, having seen him, rose up, O Bhārata, and was filled with great fear from the fierce Rakṣasa. That unseen one, fierce like death, spoke to Vasiṣṭha with a voice filled with fear. Death, fierce like a punishment, approached with a terrifying Rakṣasa, having seized him. To ward him off, there is no one else in the world, O great one, among all the knower of the Vedas. Therefore, O Lord, save me from this sin, from the red-eyed one. The Rakṣasa surely intends to devour us here.

English: Vasiṣṭha said: "Do not be afraid, O daughter, you should not fear the demon at all. This is not the fear of a demon that you see before you." King Kalmaṣapāda, renowned for his valor on earth, resides in this forest, exceedingly terrifying. The Gandharva said: Seeing him approaching, the great sage Vasiṣṭha, the Lord, prevented him with his brilliance. With the water, he again drenched him, liberating him from the terrible demon, the best of kings. For twelve years, he was indeed consumed by the brilliance of Vasiṣṭha, like the sun in the sky during the time of the wind. Freed from the demon, the king then shone with great brilliance, like the sun emerging from the evening mist. Then, having regained consciousness, he saluted with folded hands and spoke to the great sage Vasiṣṭha. "O great one, I am the son of Daśaratha, the best of the twice-born. In this matter, whatever you desire, tell me what I should do for you." Vasiṣṭha said:

He indeed filled that city, the best of the prosperous.

English: In Ayodhya, the cool moon rose like in autumn, adorned with a flag and surrounded by a path of mixed rain. The mind was delighted by that excellent city, filled with prosperous and happy people, O Kurunandana. At that time, it shone like Amarāvatī, graced by Indra. Then, upon the arrival of the king, that city was born from his friend. By the command of the king, the goddess approached Vasiṣṭha. The great sage Ṛtavā, along with her, was born. By the divine arrangement of the goddess, Vasiṣṭha, the foremost sage, was present. Then, in that city, a womb arose, and the best of sages, honored by the king, went back to his hermitage. The long-held womb did not break when the divine being was in it. Then, after a long time, a son was born, named Aramaka, who was the king and the one who established the lineage.

English: For the destruction of all worlds, the great-minded one deliberated. Then, the great-souled and great-austerity Vasiṣṭha restrained him for a reason; listen to that. Vasiṣṭha said: The king, known as Kṛtavīrya, became renowned; he was a performer of sacrifices and a scholar of the Vedas, a ruler among the Bhṛgus. He, the one who seized the earth, performed austerities with wealth and grains. At that time, the king, while engaged in his own affairs, found that the wealth of his lineage was present. Knowing the abundance of the Bhṛgus, the kings, all together, approached that great being. Some, knowing the earth, gave wealth without loss; some, fearing the Kṣatriyas, gave to their own kin. But some of the Bhṛgus gave wealth as desired to the Kṣatriyas, due to the sight of other causes. Then, by chance, the Kṣatriya dug up wealth from the earth. That wealth was seen by all. Out of anger, he then insulted those who had come.

English: The Maheshwas fasted, except for the arrows. They cut through the earth like the Gabhodana. When the Bhṛgus were being destroyed, they fled in fear. The Bhṛgupalyas reached the snowy mountain, Himavanta. Among them, the most powerful was the one with the radiant womb, who, with one thigh, increased the lineage. They saw her shining externally with her own radiance. Then Gabhah, like the sun at noon, emerged from the external form of Prats, burning the Kshatriyas. Then they, separated, wandered in confusion. Then, in fear, the Kshatriya bulls, with futile resolve, sought refuge with the Brahmani, that unblemished one. The Kshatriyas, with their minds agitated, saw the great fortunate one, like flames of fire, bringing peace from suffering. By the grace of the goddess, let the Kshatri be seen with clear vision. Let us go, having rested, along with those who have committed sins. O mother, you are our refuge, how can you abandon us all? By giving back again, you should protect the king.

English: Brahma said: "I do not grasp the object; my vision is filled with anger. This indeed is the great one, surely angry with you today." "With this eye, surely the great soul, remembering his relatives, does not doubt to take them." "When you, the sons of Bhrigu, strike the cow, then this great one is indeed held by me." "The six limbs of the Vedas indeed entered this great one, desiring the welfare of the Bhrigu lineage." "This one, surely desiring to kill, is not without anger due to the paternal vow, whose divine eye has blinded you." "O father, you should request this great son of mine; he will surely be pleased by your prostration and will release you from your affliction." The Gandharva said: "Thus addressed, all the kings then spoke to that great one, 'Be pleased,' and he granted them his grace." "By this very name, he became renowned as the best among the sorrowful; thus, the sage, breaking the bonds, revealed himself." "Having obtained the eye, the kings then returned."

English: Rye Chaitrarathapavana Bhārgava, the sage, perceived the downfall of the world. He heated the beings, both divine and human, With great austerity, he would please his grandfather. Then, knowing the best of the Bhṛgus, the fathers approached him, Saying, "O son of HARE, You have been affected by the power of your great austerity; Grant the worlds grace and control your anger." English: When the anger of the lowly Kṣatriyas of the Bhṛgu clan arose in the world, then I was filled with anger. The full treasury of my parents was not accessible due to fear in all worlds. At that time, a certain one, having taken the form of a woman, held me with a great embrace. When there is a prohibition against sin in the world, then sin does not arise in all worlds. When, however, the sinner does not obtain the one who prohibits sin, many remain in the world, then engaged in sinful acts. Even knowing, if one does not restrain sin, the Lord also is engaged in action by that very sin. If the kings and the Lord are my fathers, then they are capable of saving me with blood, considering this life to be dear. Therefore, I am angry with these beings today, and I cannot bear to act according to your words. And may this great Lord of mine also be indifferent to the sins of the worlds. And whoever desires to take away my anger, let him burn me with his own energy.

English: I know your desire to protect all beings. Therefore, let the lords of the worlds bestow what is beneficial. The fathers said: He who wishes to take away the sorrow of the worlds, let him release you, for you are established in the waters. The waters are the essence of all that exists. Therefore, let us release this anger in the waters, O best of the twice-born. Let this remain with you, O sage, if you wish for the great ocean. The anger of the man who wishes to take away the worlds is indeed the waters. Thus, this promise is true; it will surely come to pass. The worlds will not fall into destruction. Vasiṣṭha said: Then, O son of the ocean, he who is angry released the great ocean. Having become great, as the wise know, he who drinks the waters of the great ocean. Therefore, you too should not harm the worlds, O best among the knowledgeable.

English: Arjuna said: By the king Kalmaṣapāda, the best of the teachers among the knowers of Brahman, what is the reason for the fear that has been set in motion? Knowing the supreme dharma, why did that great soul not come? All was done by him earlier when asked. Gandhavva said: O Dhananjaya, understand this which you are asking me about the difficult king Vasiṣṭha and the enemy. I have told you before how that king was obtained by the great soul Vasiṣṭha. He, having obtained the kingdom, went to the city of the king Parantapa. Going to the desolate forest, he wandered about with his wife, amidst various groups of animals and diverse beings. Covered with various bushes and trees, the forest was filled with terrible sounds, and he wandered about there.

English: He, once disturbed, hunted for his own sustenance. The Brāhmaṇī and the Brāhmaṇa were united for procreation. Then, having observed, he was frightened and fled. He seized the brāhmaṇa who was running away. The wife took hold of her husband and spoke to him, "Listen, O king, I shall tell you what you should do." You are indeed renowned in the world as the son of the sun. You should not commit a sin, for you have reached the invincible. In the season of mating, they have arrived. I, having been unproductive, am indeed great in my delivery. Be pleased, O best of kings, let my husband be released. Thus, while she was crying out, the cruel one devoured her husband like a tiger would a desired prey. Overcome by her rage, she fell to the ground. That fire became a blaze and illuminated the land. Then, she, tormented by grief, was angry with the king and the Brāhmaṇa. Because of you, who are cruel and insignificant, I have been devoured today by the one of great fame.

English: Therefore, you too, being surrounded by my fish, will give up your life with compassion after reaching the land of the dead. By whom the sons of the best of the sages have been saved by you, he will unite with your brother and will give birth to a son. He will be the progenitor of the lowly king. Thus, the auspicious one spoke to the king, and he, being present, shone brightly like a fire. Vasiṣṭha, the great sage, knew all this through great knowledge and yoga, and through penance, O scorcher of enemies. The king, freed from the curse, was then greatly troubled by the intoxication that had fallen upon him. Indeed, the king, being enchanted by the curse, did not remember it. Hearing the words of the goddess, he, the best of kings, remembering that curse, was greatly distressed at that time. For this reason, the king appointed Vasiṣṭha, afflicted by the curse, in his own house, O best of Bharata.

English: Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Those who have come from the many chariots, brothers of the divine beings, should indeed know that they are accompanied by maternal relatives." "Today, let us go to the residence of the Pāñcālas, where the great Swayamvara will take place, and it will be a grand event." "We have come here for a single purpose; there will indeed be a wonderful festival there." "The daughter of Yajñasena, the great-souled Drupada, born from the altar, with a gaze like a lotus petal." "A young maiden, flawless and delicate, the sister of the mighty Drona, who is renowned for her prowess." "Born with a golden arm, with a strong body, shining like fire." "Her sister, Draupadī, of medium stature, whose fragrance is like that of a blue lotus." "Let us go to the Swayamvara of the daughter of Yajñasena, to that great divine festival." "Kings and royal sons, generous in offerings, devoted to study, pure-hearted, and with great vows."

English: The young women from various regions will come together. The great charioteers will arrive, having prepared the ground. There, the kings will offer various gifts and food for the purpose of victory. Having received all of that, we will go to the self-choice ceremony, having experienced the festival as desired. The dancers, the spirits, and the bards will also come from different regions, the mighty ones. Thus, having made arrangements, we will receive everything, and we, the great souls, will return again. O you, who are in the form of swans, looking at Krishna, let him choose the best among the gathered. This brother of yours, O illustrious one, is a great warrior, striving for victory with great wealth. Yudhishthira said: "Let us go to see the great festival of the gods, along with everyone, to the self-choice ceremony."

English: Thus spoke (the sage) Uvāca. Thus addressed, the Pāṇḍavas departed, protected by King Dakhinapāśchāla and Drupada. Then they, the great-souled, pure-hearted, and sinless Pāṇḍavas, honored the sage Vyāsa appropriately and were consoled by him. After that, they were permitted to proceed towards the land of Drupada. They enjoyed beautiful forests and lakes along the way, and there, the charioteers also arrived. Being engaged in self-study, pure, and sweet-tongued, they reached the Pāñcālas, the descendants of Kuru. The Pāṇḍavas then settled in the city of Skandhāvāra, in the house of the potter. There, they took to a livelihood of collecting alms, and they received what was offered to them. The desire of Yajñasena was for the Pāṇḍava with the crown; he always sought Krishna, and if he did not, he would not be fulfilled. While searching for him, the Kuntīyas, the Pāṇḍavas, made the earth tremble.
